lesson.title: How Water Climbs Against Gravity
lesson.summary: Capillary action is the rise of a liquid up a narrow tube against gravity, driven by a balance between adhesive forces pulling the liquid toward the tube's walls and cohesive forces, including hydrogen bonding, holding the liquid together as it climbs.
lesson.body:
Capillary action is the ability of a liquid to flow upward through a narrow tube or a narrow space, apparently against gravity, without any external pump or pressure driving it. It arises from a competition between two kinds of intermolecular attraction acting at once: adhesive forces, the attraction between the liquid's molecules and the surface of the tube itself, and cohesive forces, the attraction between the liquid's own molecules holding it together, the same cohesive forces responsible for surface tension. When the adhesive forces between the liquid and the tube's surface are stronger than the liquid's own cohesive forces, the liquid is pulled up along the tube walls; as that thin film of liquid climbs the walls, cohesive forces between liquid molecules drag the rest of the liquid column up behind it, and the surface tension at the top of the liquid resists breaking, so the whole column rises together rather than only a thin film climbing alone.

Water in a narrow glass tube is the standard demonstration. Glass surfaces are covered with oxygen atoms in silicon-oxygen bonds that carry a partial negative charge, and these can form hydrogen bonds with the hydrogen atoms of water molecules, since a hydrogen atom bonded directly to oxygen in water is exactly the kind of hydrogen bond donor described under hydrogen bond requirements. Because this adhesion between water and glass, driven substantially by hydrogen bonding, is stronger than water's cohesion to itself, water climbs the inside walls of a glass tube and produces the concave meniscus mentioned when discussing surface tension. The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid climbs, because the ratio of the tube's wall surface area, where adhesion acts, to the volume of liquid that has to be lifted becomes more favorable in a thinner tube; this is why capillary action is barely noticeable in a drinking glass but very obvious in a narrow glass capillary tube only a fraction of a millimeter wide.

Not every liquid experiences capillary action the same way, and mercury is the clearest counterexample. Mercury atoms are held together by strong metallic bonding among themselves, cohesive forces that are much stronger than any adhesive attraction mercury can form with glass. Because cohesion dominates over adhesion in that case, mercury does not climb a glass tube at all; instead it is pulled down slightly at the walls, producing a convex meniscus that curves the opposite way from water's. Comparing water and mercury side by side is a useful check on the underlying logic: capillary action height and direction depend entirely on which of the two forces, adhesion to the container or cohesion within the liquid, wins out, not on some general tendency of all liquids to rise in narrow spaces.

Capillary action is not just a laboratory curiosity; it is one of the mechanisms that moves water upward through the narrow xylem vessels of trees and plants, helping carry water from the roots toward the leaves, working alongside other physical processes like transpiration. Paper towels and cloth wicking up spilled liquid, and ink climbing through a thin chromatography strip, both rely on the same balance of adhesion, cohesion, and narrow channel geometry. In every one of these cases, the underlying explanation traces back to the same two forces introduced here, both of which ultimately depend on the intermolecular forces, particularly hydrogen bonding in the case of water, that were built up over the course of this entire unit.
